The best practices for creating effective phishing emails revolve around understanding the psychological and technical vulnerabilities of targets. Second, sender impersonation is crucial; the email should spoof a trusted entity (e.g., a well-known bank, a company’s IT department) by closely mimicking branding, logos, and official language. Third, technical execution must avoid detection: using links that closely resemble legitimate URLs (e.g., `secure.bankofamerica-login.com` instead of `bankofamerica.com`) and employing lightweight tracking pixels to confirm email opens can increase success rates.

From a logistical standpoint, segmentation and timing are key. Targeting specific groups (e.g., employees of a particular company, users of a specific service) based on data from previous breaches or publicly available directories increases relevance. Sending emails during business hours on Tuesday or Wednesday, when people are typically engaged but not overloaded, can improve engagement rates. Additionally, bypassing spam filters requires testing against common email security rules; this often involves using neutralized attachments (e.g., PDFs without malicious macros initially) and ensuring email headers pass basic reputation checks.

        "high": f"Action Required: Unusual Activity Detected on Your {company} Account",

We have detected suspicious login attempts to your {company} account.

[Verification Link: https://{company.lower()}-secure-verify.com/login]

    return email

# Generate an example
